accuracy.evidence: Checked against the Natural History Museum pages on hoverflies (harmless Batesian mimics of wasps and bees, no sting) and on stick and leaf insects (twig and leaf masquerade, keeping still and swaying), Royal Entomological Society fact sheets (true flies have one pair of wings; wasps and bees two pairs; only females sting), Butterfly Conservation on the cinnabar moth (caterpillars take up ragwort alkaloids and carry yellow and black warning stripes), the Wildlife Trusts on the wasp beetle (harmless wasp mimic), ladybird reflex bleeding of bitter alkaloids, and Ruxton, Sherratt and Speed (2004) on predators learning aposematic signals after one or a few unpleasant encounters. The drone fly is a well-known honeybee mimic. Parameterised answers a-b, 4*a+2*b, b and b-2 stay positive whole numbers at every corner of their ranges.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented slips (Jungwirth 1975 and Bishop and Anderson 1990 on intentional, need-driven adaptation; common confusion of hoverflies with wasps in public-engagement studies): every stripy insect stings (predict 3, the copycat cards, p4, m1, challenge 'sting'), bright colours make prey easy to find (predict 2, robot saying 1, p3, challenge 'bright'), hiding is about colour alone (predict 1, wrong-place feedback naming shape and colour, robot saying 3, challenge 'still'), birds are born knowing (robot saying 4, m5, challenge 'learn') and insects choose their looks (robot saying 5, m8).

lab_distinct.evidence: Each scene is about this topic's three strategies in insects: masquerade matching (stick insect to twig, leaf insect to leaf, thorn bug to thorn, peppered moth to bark) by tap or drag, a predator-learning game where the bird's memory bar fills with each sting and later wasps are refused, a judge-the-stinger round with wing-count and waist clues for six real model and mimic species, and a hide/warn/copy sort. flagcamo (529) recolours a moth and moves a hare across backgrounds, flaghunt (874) is predator hunting tricks and flagvary (885) is variation over generations; none has predator learning or mimics. The lab_distinct gate keeps flag_mimic.js under 30% similar to every other lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner discovers by doing: putting an insect on the wrong plant part gets feedback naming the mismatched shape and colour; in the bird game the first two wasps sting and fill the memory bar, after which tapping a wasp shows the bird leaving it alone, so the learner sees that warning colours work because predators learn and that two wasps paid the price; the copycat round gives the wing and waist clue before the answer so the learner judges from evidence; the sort feedback says why a wrong box fails (an honest warning versus a copy).

predictions.evidence: Three predictions with tempting wrong options the lab then disproves: what helps a stick insect hide (bright colours), why a wasp is yellow and black (so birds can find it to eat) and whether a striped hoverfly can sting (yes, stripes mean it stings). Each step's completion message names the learner's own prediction against the result.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Seven rotating questions, each with two tagged wrong answers. why() has five distinct messages that name the slip: bright (bright colours are a warning, birds learn), sting (a hoverfly is a fly with no sting, its stripes copy a wasp), still (a stick insect hides by shape and stillness, not speed), learn (birds are not born knowing; a sting or nasty taste teaches them) and clue (stripes and flowers fool us; count the wings, 2 for flies and 4 for wasps and bees).

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs use short sentences and plain words (hide, warn, copy, sting, twig) with each technical word introduced once by meaning (camouflage, warning colours, mimicry) and pass the kid limit; the adult paragraphs pass the adult limit while naming aposematism and Batesian mimicry. Canvas card labels shrink to fit at 360 px and all text is dark on white, pale green or pale red.

no_filler.evidence: Kid paragraph 1 states the three tricks, then one paragraph each for camouflage, warning colours with predator learning, and mimicry with the wing-count clue. Adult text gives key words, the mechanisms with named species, three named mistakes and what the lab does. The content gate found no filler phrases and under 12% overlap with every other lesson, including 529 Animal camouflage.

mobile.evidence: Checked iPhone 13 dark screenshots part-way through each Show me: the four insects sit in a row above a 2 x 2 grid of plant parts with the hidden insect drawn on its place, the bird game uses a 4 x 2 grid of 100 px tiles under a full-width memory bar, the copycat card fills three quarters of the width above 70 px answer keys, and the sort uses a 3 x 2 grid above three large Hide, Warn and Copy boxes. Nothing clips at 390 px.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a labelled button twin: pick each insect then 'On the twig' and so on (named with the insect), 'Peck 1' to 'Peck 8' each labelled with what the insect is, Can sting or Copycat named with the insect, pick then Hide, Warn or Copy, and Right or Slip. Every result is spoken via c.say and the canvas aria-label, challenge feedback is in a polite live region, and correctness is always given in words as well as colour. The walk gate's axe run was clean in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13.
